The Committee’s rate cut to 1.50–1.75% and the directive to purchase Treasury bills and conduct repos to keep reserves ample are consistent with evidence that easing works through liquidity and credit channels to support real activity. In particular, maintaining low short‑term funding costs reinforces the liquidity effect and policy transmission (Sims; McCallum & Nelson), while alleviating financing constraints that are especially binding for business fixed and inventory investment (Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein, 1994)—a timely response to the noted weakness in investment and exports. With overall and core inflation below 2% and inflation compensation subdued, New Keynesian estimates of inflation dynamics (Galí, Gertler, and López‑Salido; Rudebusch) imply that, given anchored expectations and modest slack, accommodation is appropriate to move inflation toward the symmetric 2% objective. Empirical work using VAR and structural models (Sims; Zha) indicates such easing tends to lift real activity in the near term, aligning with the Committee’s baseline of sustained expansion, though the split vote highlights residual uncertainty around the outlook and calibration.
